| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wp-content\\plugins\\content-delivery-helper\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wp-content\\plugins\\database-optimizer\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
WordPress PHP process spawning shell from wp-content directory AIExploitation Medium
Detects php / php-fpm / php-cgi processes whose working directory or invoking script path resolves under wp-content spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe / bash / sh — the canonical web-shell execution shape for the hidden Sansec backdoor. Rationale: The article says the hidden plugin opens a web shell — 'anyone who knows the right URL can run code on the server.' On a WordPress host, that materialises as php / php-fpm spawning a shell or curl/wget. Anchoring on the wp-content / wp-admin path eliminates generic PHP CLI scripts. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress CLI tools (wp-cli) running maintenance tasks that legitimately spawn curl for plugin updates
  • Backup plugins (UpdraftPlus, BackupBuddy) shelling out to tar/gzip from wp-content/uploads
  • Image-processing plugins invoking imagemagick / ffmpeg via shell wrappers
  • Cron-scheduled WordPress jobs that pull remote feeds via curl from wp-content paths
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","updraftplus","backupbuddy","wp-cron.php") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tar","gzip","rsync"))
Response runbook
1. Triage — capture the full process chain (grandparent → parent → child) and the script path resolved from the PHP CLI args. Identify which WordPress plugin owns the parent path. 2. Contain — kill the offending PHP worker, quarantine the parent script file, and add a temporary egress block for the host to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54. 3. Hunt — pivot on the same DeviceId for content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer folder writes, rogue developer_api1 / dev_* admin accounts, and inbound HTTP requests for the script path in web-server access logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d", "FromBase64String", "eval(", "system(", "passthru(")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin","wp-includes")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])php(-cgi|-fpm)?(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|bash|sh|dash|zsh|nc|ncat|curl(\.exe)?|wget(\.exe)?)$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d","FromBase64String","eval(","system(","passthru(")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin","wp-includes")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=ActorUsername,
          Parent=ParentProcessName, ParentCmd=ParentProcessCommandLine,
          Child=ActingProcessName, ChildCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PHP process spawning shell from WordPress directory
id: 8e5d6f7a-4b3c-4d8e-9a2f-3c4d5e6f7a04
description: Detects php / php-fpm / php-cgi spawning a shell or download utility while running with wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes in its path or command line — the canonical Sansec backdoor web-shell execution pattern.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php'
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php-cgi'
      - '\php.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
  selection_path:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'wp-content'
      - 'wp-admin'
      - 'wp-includes'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_path
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) AND @ParentImage:(*\php.exe OR *\PHP.EXE OR */php OR */php-fpm OR */php-cgi) AND @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR */bash OR */sh OR */dash OR */curl OR */wget OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe) AND @ParentCommandLine:(*wp-content* OR *wp-admin* OR *wp-includes*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^php(-cgi|-fpm)?(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|[\\\/](bash|sh|dash|zsh|nc|ncat|curl|wget))(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(?i)(wp-content|wp-admin|wp-includes)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs · [LLM] User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.

Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs AIDelivery High
Inbound message contains a URL pointing to known Sniper Dz redirector or landing-page infrastructure (sniperdz.com, raviral.com, win.feezossl.xyz, etc.). Hunts the delivery vector even when the lure was originally posted on Facebook and forwarded to the victim via mail share. Group-IB tied these domains to the post-INTERPOL-takedown resurgence of the kit. Rationale: Uses the specific IOC domains the article enumerates as Sniper Dz infrastructure. Inbound + URL-domain match on a curated list is high-fidelity because these are not generic services; the only FP risk is a security analyst forwarding the IOC list internally.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst forwarding the IOC list or Group-IB write-up via email
  • Threat-intel digest emails that quote the URLs verbatim (Recorded Future, Group-IB newsletter)
  • Phishing-simulation vendor URLs that intentionally mimic these domains for awareness training
  • User reporting the phishing email back through a Report Phish add-in (causes the same URL to traverse the wire again)
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromAddress !endswith "@yourorg.com" and RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("soc@yourorg.com","phishing-reports@yourorg.com","abuse@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full recipient list for the matching NetworkMessageId via EmailEvents and check whether any of them subsequently appear in UrlClickEvents for the same NetworkMessageId — that escalates this from delivery to click-through. Step 2 (contain): soft-delete or quarantine outstanding copies via Defender Threat Explorer for the NetworkMessageId, and add the matched UrlDomain values to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents on the same domains for the last 14 days across the recipient population to find anyone who opened the URL outside Safe Links (clicked from mobile, copy-pasted into another browser).
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | extend HostLower = tolower(UrlDomain)
    | where HostLower has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Url has_any (SniperDzDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, ReportId
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Proofpoint","Mimecast","Cisco","Microsoft")
| where RequestURL has_any (SniperDzDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Message has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, Activity, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) AIDelivery High
Safe Links UrlClickEvents for one of the Sniper Dz infrastructure domains, including ClickedThrough where the user bypassed the warning. This is the highest-fidelity post-delivery signal in the kill chain and the one that warrants immediate user contact, because the next step in the article's described funnel is browser-notification permission grant and TDS routing. Rationale: UrlClickEvents is the only Defender table that confirms the user actually opened the link (vs. it merely landed in their inbox). IsClickedThrough==true is an extra escalation signal because Safe Links warned them and they proceeded anyway — high-priority user-contact case. Domains are taken verbatim from the article's IOC list. Sentinel has no equivalent table without M365 Defender, so sentinel_kql is intentionally empty.
ATT&CKT1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually clicking the URL inside Safe Links during triage of UC1
  • Phishing-reporter user clicking the link before reporting (legitimate but operationally noisy)
  • Web-content categorisation services that crawl through Safe Links
  • Sandbox / detonation vendor accounts that follow URLs from quarantined mail
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("soc-analyst@yourorg.com","ir-handler@yourorg.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known-sandbox-egress-ips>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify AccountUpn and pull DeviceInfo to map to device; pull DeviceNetworkEvents on the user's primary device for the 30 min after ClickTime — look for follow-on traffic to the redirect chain or notification-service VAPID endpoints. Step 2 (contain): reset the user's session cookies for the mail tenant and force MFA re-prompt; if the user reports they granted browser-notification permission, push a managed-browser policy that revokes notification grants for the IOC domains. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the matched Url back to EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo on the same NetworkMessageId to identify the original sender and other recipients; check for secondary clicks from the same campaign within 24h across the tenant.
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by Timestamp desc

DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) AICommand & Control Medium
Direct EDR/DNS observation of a workstation contacting one of the Sniper Dz hosting IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) or attempting to resolve one of the named scam domains. Catches the case where the user reached the link outside Safe Links (mobile mail, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser) and only the network egress survives. Rationale: Article enumerates three IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) and nine domains as the campaign's hosting / redirect / TDS infrastructure. IP-membership + DNS-query-name match is the cleanest IOC pivot available and survives the scenario where Safe Links never observed the click (mobile, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser).

Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion box pulling the same IOCs from an OSINT source (e.g. abuse.ch fetch)
  • Researcher sandbox detonating the URLs from a corporate egress
  • URL-scanning service (urlscan, VirusTotal) called from an internal pipeline that resolves IOC domains
  • Pantheonsite.io is shared-tenant hosting — false positives possible if dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io is later reassigned to a legitimate customer (revalidate domain ownership quarterly)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<threat-intel-sandbox-hostnames>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-threatintel","svc-urlscan")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the device, the user, and the originating process — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (msedge.exe/chrome.exe/firefox.exe) check UrlClickEvents and EmailEvents for the same user within the prior 30 min to identify the lure source; if it's a non-browser process, treat as elevated severity. Step 2 (contain): block the IPs at perimeter and the domains in the secure web gateway / DNS resolver; revoke browser notification permission via managed policy for affected users. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the user across DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents for related redirect domains (Linktree / Linkbio destinations that ended in the same IPs), and across the wider population for any device that resolved any of the IOC domains in the last 30 days.
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (SniperDzIPs)
   or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and tolower(RemoteUrl) has_any (SniperDzDomains))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where tolower(Name) has_any (SniperDzDomains)

  | where tolower(DnsQuery) has_any (SniperDzDomains)

( CommonSecurityLog

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'

Palo Alto Warns of Active Exploitation of PAN-OS GlobalProtect VPN Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks has revealed that it has observed "active exploitation" of a recently disclosed PAN-OS vulnerability by an unknown threat actor to obtain unauthorized access to GlobalProtect portals. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw affecting the portal and gateway components of PAN-OS software that could be exploited by bad

CVEsCVE-2026-0257

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] GlobalProtect Gateway/Portal Traffic From CVE-2026-0257 Attack Infrastructure IPs
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect PoC Client-Config Signature (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain) · [LLM] GlobalProtect Session With CVE-2026-0257 PoC Default Hostnames (WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001 / DESKTOP-GP01 / GP-CLIENT) · [LLM] GlobalProtect Session Reporting Vendor-Default Placeholder MAC Address
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect PoC Client-Config Signature (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain) AIExploitation High
Hunts the article's primary detection guidance: successful GlobalProtect gateway-connected events whose client posture carries the hard-coded PoC values endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' AND empty source_user_info.domain. Real users almost never connect with both an empty domain and that exact Win10 Pro string simultaneously. Rationale: Uses the two PoC client-config strings Palo Alto Networks explicitly told customers to search for in GlobalProtect logs (endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' + empty source_user_info.domain). Both conditions together are essentially unique to the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest replay of the public PoC against a corporate GP gateway during an authorized assessment
  • Engineering test rigs imaged with a generic Win10 Pro template and joined to no AD domain (workgroup laptops)
  • Lab/QA GlobalProtect clients used by network engineers validating gateway upgrades with default client builds
  • Legitimate BYOD / contractor laptop running Windows 10 Pro never joined to a domain
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ('pentest-svc', 'redteam-lab', 'gp-test') | where SourceIP !in ('10.0.0.0/8', '192.168.0.0/16')
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP and SourceUserName from the hit and confirm whether the account is real, whether it normally connects from a domain-joined endpoint, and whether the source IP appears in the article's IOC list. 2) Contain: revoke active GlobalProtect sessions for the user, force a password+MFA reset, and block the source IP at the perimeter firewall pending investigation. Verify the appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across firewall, IIS, and AAD logs for the past 60 days; look for additional gateway-connected events from the same IP under other usernames (credential spray pattern), and search internal traffic from the VPN-assigned IP for reconnaissance behaviour even though Palo Alto Networks reports no post-access activity yet.

| where Message has 'Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit'
| where Message has 'source_user_info.domain='
| where Message has_any ('source_user_info.domain=;', 'source_user_info.domain= ', 'source_user_info.domain=,', 'source_user_info.domain=|', 'source_user_info.domain=empty')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect PoC Client-Config Signature
id: 7a3b8c41-9e2d-4f12-b8c5-1d9e4a7b6c3f
description: Detects successful GlobalProtect gateway-connected events that carry the hard-coded PoC client posture from CVE-2026-0257 exploitation (endpoint_os_version 'Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' combined with an empty source_user_info.domain).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15

  - attack.initial_access

logsource:
  product: paloalto
  service: globalprotect
detection:

    event_type: gateway-connected
    endpoint_os_version: 'Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit'
  empty_domain:
    source_user_info.domain:
      - ''
      - '-'
      - 'empty'
  condition: selection and empty_domain
level: high
source:pan-os "gateway-connected" "Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit" "source_user_info.domain="
NETWORK
`pan_globalprotect` event_type=gateway-connected endpoint_os_version="Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit"
| eval domain_empty=if(isnull(source_user_info_domain) OR source_user_info_domain="" OR source_user_info_domain="-" OR source_user_info_domain=="empty", 1, 0)
| where domain_empty=1
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime count values(public_ip) as public_ip values(source_user) as source_user values(machinename) as machinename by src_ip endpoint_os_version source_user_info_domain
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
GlobalProtect Gateway/Portal Traffic From CVE-2026-0257 Attack Infrastructure IPs AIDelivery Medium
Watches firewall + endpoint telemetry for any traffic involving the nine IP addresses Palo Alto Networks attributed to active CVE-2026-0257 exploitation. Hits represent either inbound exploitation attempts against your GP portal or outbound traffic from an internal host to the same infrastructure. Rationale: Direct hard match against the nine IOC IPs Palo Alto Networks published as confirmed CVE-2026-0257 attack infrastructure. Inbound hits = exploitation attempt; outbound from internal hosts = potential beacon to attacker infra. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN-related troubleshooting / TAC support sessions where an engineer connects out to one of the IPs to validate the IOC list
  • Researcher / threat-hunter VM in your network actively probing the listed IPs for IOC enrichment
  • Stale NAT or shared-hosting reuse — one of the IPs is later assigned to a benign cloud customer your users legitimately reach
  • Honeypot or sandbox infrastructure your team operates that happens to share an IP range
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('threathunter.exe', 'curl.exe', 'powershell_ise.exe') | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ('threat-research', 'soc-analyst')
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction — inbound to the GP portal or outbound from an internal endpoint. For inbound, confirm whether any of the same IPs produced a successful gateway-connected event in the last 30 days. For outbound, identify the source host and process. 2) Contain: block all nine IPs at the perimeter firewall and at any cloud egress gateway; if outbound, isolate the source endpoint immediately and preserve memory. 3) Hunt: search 60 days of firewall + proxy + DNS for any historical contact with these IPs; pull GlobalProtect logs for all successful gateway-connected events from these IPs and correlate to the PoC-signature detection above; check whether any of the source IPs probed other public services in your perimeter.

GlobalProtect Session With CVE-2026-0257 PoC Default Hostnames (WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001 / DESKTOP-GP01 / GP-CLIENT) AIExploitation High
Detects gateway-connected GlobalProtect events whose reported client hostname matches the three textbook PoC defaults disclosed by Palo Alto Networks. No real enterprise asset inventory contains these exact names. Rationale: These three hostnames are PoC scaffolding values explicitly named in the article's IOC list — they are functionally indistinguishable from canaries. A real client almost never reports these as its NetBIOS/host_id. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1133 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly imaged corporate laptop that hasn't received its asset-tag rename yet (rare; investigate anyway)
  • QA / staging GlobalProtect test client a network engineer named generically
  • Cloud-based VDI golden image whose hostname template literally happens to be DESKTOP-GP01
  • Asset built from an off-the-shelf Win10 install with the installer-generated default DESKTOP-XXXXXXX placeholder
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP and SourceUserName for each hit. Look up the username in IAM/HR — is the account active, and does the user own a real corporate laptop? Check whether the public_ip overlaps with the nine known attacker IPs. 2) Contain: kill the GP session, disable the account pending investigation, and block the source public IP. 3) Hunt: search 90 days for any prior gateway-connected event using the same hostname against any account; pivot on the SourceIP to find other compromised accounts; cross-check with the PoC-signature detection (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain).
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceName in~ ('WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001', 'DESKTOP-GP01', 'GP-CLIENT')
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, IsAzureADJoined
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where Message has_any ('WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001', 'DESKTOP-GP01', 'GP-CLIENT')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects GlobalProtect gateway-connected events whose client hostname matches the textbook PoC defaults disclosed for CVE-2026-0257 exploitation.

detection:

      - 'WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001'

      - 'GP-CLIENT'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:pan-os "gateway-connected" ("WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001" OR "DESKTOP-GP01" OR "GP-CLIENT")
NETWORK
`pan_globalprotect` event_type=gateway-connected (machinename="WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001" OR machinename="DESKTOP-GP01" OR machinename="GP-CLIENT" OR host_id="WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001" OR host_id="DESKTOP-GP01" OR host_id="GP-CLIENT")
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime count values(public_ip) as public_ip values(source_user) as source_user values(endpoint_os_version) as endpoint_os_version by machinename src_ip

GlobalProtect Session Reporting Vendor-Default Placeholder MAC Address AIExploitation High
Hunts GlobalProtect HIP / host-info logs for the two textbook placeholder MAC addresses listed in the IOC bundle (aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and 00:11:22:33:44:55). Real NICs ship with manufacturer-assigned OUIs; these values are unmistakable PoC artifacts. Rationale: Both MAC addresses are explicit IOCs from Palo Alto Networks' bundle and have OUIs that no real NIC manufacturer owns — aa:bb:cc and 00:11:22 are classic documentation/placeholder values used in the PoC client spoofing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1133 T1036
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester using a tool that doesn't randomise MACs and ships with the same documentation defaults
  • Network engineer running GlobalProtect from a Hyper-V/VirtualBox guest whose virtual NIC was assigned a manually-typed placeholder MAC during lab setup
  • Asset-management or HIP-misconfiguration where the agent fails to read the real MAC and falls back to a default
  • Threat-research VM in your environment that emulates the PoC client for IOC validation
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP, SourceUserName and timestamp for each hit. Confirm whether the same session also reported the PoC OS string or one of the cookie-cutter hostnames — multiple PoC indicators together is near-certain exploitation. 2) Contain: terminate the GP session, disable the account, block the source public IP, and force a credential reset. 3) Hunt: search 90 days for any other sessions reporting these MACs against any account; pivot on the public_ip to find sibling sessions; correlate against the PAN advisory for newer IOCs and confirm the appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where Message has_any ('aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff', '00:11:22:33:44:55')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, SourceMACAddress, DestinationMACAddress, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

—

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Velvet Ant GS-Netcat C2 relay lookup to gs.thc.org AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or outbound network connections to gs.thc.org (the hard-coded relay used by Velvet Ant's modified GS-Netcat/gsocket reverse shell). Production Linux servers — especially internet-facing Nginx/web tier hosts — have no legitimate reason to contact the THC global socket relay; a single hit is high-fidelity initial-foothold or post-compromise C2 evidence for Operation Highland. Rationale: gs.thc.org is the hard-coded relay domain Velvet Ant's modified GS-Netcat connects to (named in the BleepingComputer article and corroborated by Sygnia's blog and The Hacker News write-up). Production Linux servers have no benign reason to touch THC's global socket relay, so a single resolution is high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-hackers-backdoored-linux.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team / pentest engagement legitimately using gsocket for OOB shells
  • Security researcher on a sandbox host evaluating THC tooling
  • Developer with a personal SSH-over-NAT tunnel via gsocket (rare on corporate endpoints)
  • Threat-intel feed pre-fetching DNS for IOC enrichment from the same host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("redteam-runner","breach-sim-agent") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/opt/redteam/")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull all DeviceProcessEvents on the hitting host for the 60s window around the DNS query — identify the process that initiated the lookup, its parent, and the binary hash. Check whether the host is internet-facing (Nginx/web tier — the Operation Highland foothold profile). 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host via EDR network containment; preserve /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, and the suspect binary for forensics; rotate any SSH keys and service-account credentials present on the host. 3) HUNT: pivot on the suspect process hash and filename across the estate; search DeviceFileEvents for newly written files in /etc/systemd/system/ and /usr/lib/systemd/system/ in the prior 30 days; look for sibling indicators (pam_*.so writes, sshd hash mismatches, fcgiwrap installs) — all four are part of the same Velvet Ant chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gs.thc.org" or RemoteUrl endswith ".thc.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has "gs.thc.org" or Name endswith ".thc.org"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has "gs.thc.org" or RequestURL has "gs.thc.org" or DestinationDnsDomain has "thc.org"
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has "gs.thc.org" or DnsQuery endswith ".thc.org"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velvet Ant backdoored PAM module write (pam_unix.so outside package manager) AIInstallation High
Detects creation or modification of pam_*.so files in /lib/security/, /lib64/security/, /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/ or /usr/lib64/security/ by processes that are NOT a system package manager. Operation Highland replaced pam_unix.so with one of nine backdoored variants that accept a hard-coded password and harvest credentials in flight — any non-rpm/dpkg write to these paths is a credible persistence event. Rationale: Article names nine variants of backdoored pam_unix.so dropped by Velvet Ant; Sygnia's blog confirms two variants act as a hard-coded-password backdoor and credential harvester. Filtering on path + filename + non-package-manager parent gives a near-zero-FP signal — any legitimate PAM module update would come via dpkg/rpm. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-hackers-backdoored-linux.html
ATT&CKT1556.003 T1556 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet pushing a custom pam_tally2 or pam_faillock configuration via the agent (not dpkg)
  • Vendor MFA agents (Duo, Okta Verify, Yubico pam_u2f) installer running under a custom shell script
  • Security team manually compiling and copying a hardened pam_unix.so during an incident-response exercise
  • Container-image build inside a chroot where /lib/security paths are being staged
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ansible", "puppet", "chef-client", "salt-minion") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pam_u2f", "pam_duo", "pam_oath", "pam_tally"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: hash the new pam_*.so and diff against the canonical package version (`rpm -V pam` / `dpkg -V libpam-modules` / `debsums -c`). Capture the writing process's parent chain — Velvet Ant's installs come from non-systemd, non-pkgmgr parents. 2) CONTAIN: do NOT delete the malicious .so blindly — replacing PAM modules without a tested rollback can lock all admins out (Sygnia explicitly warns about this). Snapshot the host, deploy a known-good pam_unix.so from a trusted RPM/DEB into /lib/security via a side-channel, then validate `su` and `sshd` still work before removing the host from isolation. 3) HUNT: across the estate, hash every pam_*.so and join to the package manifest — any mismatch is a candidate variant. Pivot on the writing-process hash to find sibling intrusions; also check sshd/ssh/scp binaries for tampering and search DeviceNetworkEvents for gs.thc.org callbacks from the same hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"/lib/security/", @"/lib64/security/", @"/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/", @"/usr/lib64/security/", @"/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/")
| where FileName startswith "pam_" and FileName endswith ".so"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg", "rpm", "yum", "dnf", "apt", "apt-get", "zypper", "tdnf", "unattended-upgr", "packagekitd", "rpmbuild")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/lib/apt/methods/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, MD5, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"/lib/security/", @"/lib64/security/", @"/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/", @"/usr/lib64/security/", @"/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/")
| where TargetFileName startswith "pam_" and TargetFileName endswith ".so"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg", "rpm", "yum", "dnf", "apt", "apt-get", "zypper", "tdnf", "unattended-upgr", "packagekitd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Backdoored PAM Module Write Outside Package Manager (Velvet Ant Operation Highland)
id: 7b1f9c83-2d44-4ab8-8e91-3f5a6c2b9d12
description: Detects write or replacement of pam_*.so files under /lib*/security/ by a process that is not a known package manager. Mirrors Velvet Ant's pam_unix.so backdoor installation observed in Operation Highland.
references:
  - https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-hijack-auth-flow-spy-on-isolated-network-for-a-decade/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1556.003
  - attack.t1554
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/lib/security/pam_'
      - '/lib64/security/pam_'
      - '/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_'
      - '/usr/lib64/security/pam_'
      - '/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.so'
  filter_pkgmgr:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/rpm'
      - '/yum'
      - '/dnf'
      - '/apt'
      - '/apt-get'
      - '/zypper'
      - '/tdnf'
      - '/unattended-upgrade'
      - '/packagekitd'
  condition: selection_path and not filter_pkgmgr
falsepositives:
  - Configuration management tools (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) overlaying custom PAM modules
  - Hand-built PAM modules deployed by a security/IAM team
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) (@file.path:/lib/security/pam_*.so OR @file.path:/lib64/security/pam_*.so OR @file.path:/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/pam_*.so OR @file.path:/usr/lib64/security/pam_*.so) -@process.executable.path:(/usr/bin/dpkg OR /usr/bin/rpm OR /usr/bin/yum OR /usr/bin/dnf OR /usr/bin/apt OR /usr/bin/apt-get OR /usr/bin/zypper OR /usr/lib/apt/methods/* OR /usr/bin/unattended-upgrade OR /usr/bin/packagekitd)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/(lib|lib64|usr\/lib64|usr\/lib\/x86_64-linux-gnu|lib\/x86_64-linux-gnu)\/security\/pam_[a-z0-9_]+\.so$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\/(dpkg|rpm|yum|dnf|apt|apt-get|zypper|tdnf|unattended-upgr|packagekitd)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/lib/security/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/lib64/security/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/usr/lib64/security/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/*") AND Filesystem.file_name="pam_*.so" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("dpkg","rpm","yum","dnf","apt","apt-get","zypper","tdnf","unattended-upgrade","packagekitd") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Trojanized OpenSSH binary write (ssh/sshd/scp replaced outside package manager) AIInstallation High
Detects creation or overwrite of /usr/bin/ssh, /usr/sbin/sshd, /usr/bin/scp (and sibling OpenSSH binaries) by any process that is not a known Linux package manager. Velvet Ant replaced these binaries with trojanized versions that capture credentials and log SSH session commands — a non-pkgmgr write to these specific paths is article-specific persistence and credential-access evidence. Rationale: Article specifies ssh, sshd, scp were replaced with trojanized versions that capture credentials and log session commands. Sygnia's blog confirms these are full binary replacements. Filtering on exact OpenSSH binary paths + excluding package managers makes this a clean detection — OpenSSH should only be updated via apt/yum/dnf in production. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-hackers-backdoored-linux.html
ATT&CKT1554 T1556 T1056.001 T1040
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin compiling openssh-portable from source for a hardened build and `make install` overwriting /usr/local/sbin/sshd
  • Configuration management push of a vendor-patched OpenSSH (HPN-SSH, OpenSSL FIPS rebuilds) via Ansible's `copy` module
  • Container image bake pipeline writing /usr/sbin/sshd inside a chroot during build
  • Vendor security-update script that downloads and replaces sshd directly (non-pkgmgr but legitimate vendor flow)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ansible", "puppet", "chef-client", "salt-minion", "cfengine-execd") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openssh", "hpnssh", "fips"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: compute SHA256 of the modified ssh/sshd/scp and compare against the canonical package hash (`rpm -V openssh-server` / `dpkg-query -V openssh-server` / verify against a clean image). Inspect the writing process — Velvet Ant writes from a non-systemd, non-pkgmgr context, often a generic shell script under /tmp or /var/tmp. 2) CONTAIN: do not kill sshd on the live host (it will likely also kill your incident-response session); instead snapshot the host, mark for offline-recovery, capture the malicious binary, and reinstall openssh-server from a trusted repo via an out-of-band channel. Rotate every SSH key, password, and Kerberos cred that has touched the host in the past 30+ days — credentials may already be in the local capture file. 3) HUNT: look for the local credential-capture sink (Sygnia notes data stored locally for later retrieval — check /var/tmp, /tmp, /dev/shm and uncommon dotdirs in $HOME). Pivot to sibling detections (pam_unix.so backdoor, gs.thc.org C2, fcgiwrap c
